curationNote: Full arXiv HTML reviewed. Numeric claims below are retained only when the claim ledger points to a full-text section, table, or figure; abstract-only numbers are not promoted.

row.Title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
row.Interface Domain: Browser automation and DOM event streams
row.Observation/Input: Session-level mouse, click, keyboard, scroll, timing, and browser-environment features extracted from DOM event JSONL
row.Action Channel: Physical human input for CaptchaSolve30k; Claude driving Chrome through MCP and Playwright for agent sessions; simulated bot feature vectors
row.Agent Architecture: Claude computer-use agent over Chrome/Playwright; MLP, random forest, gradient-boosted trees, XGBoost, and SAINT detectors
row.Detection/Defense Target: Three-class discrimination among human, conventional bot, and AI-agent sessions, plus robustness to trajectory-level evasion
row.Benchmark/Dataset: CaptchaSolve30k human trajectories; 5,000 simulated bot samples; 1,025 Claude/Playwright sessions on 10 tasks; five-level evasion ladder
row.Metrics: Per-class precision, recall, F1, macro-F1, confusion matrices, expected calibration error, multi-seed intervals, feature-subset performance, and evasion-level recall
row.Code/Data Available: Paper says code, models, and processed data will be released on publication; no public artifact URL was verified on 2026-08-11
row.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium after release: feature definitions and protocols are detailed, but the human and agent classes are not task-matched and the announced artifacts are not yet public
row.Key Takeaway: The observed detector primarily separates Playwright's DOM-event emission pattern from physical input, not agent reasoning. The strong result is therefore executor-specific evidence, while task-domain mismatch and missing OS-level input simulation limit broader human-versus-agent claims.
row.Notes/Blockers: Humans solve CAPTCHAs while agents perform ten different web tasks; Section 8 is an ablation rather than a matched-task human study. The paper excludes OS-level simulation such as PyAutoGUI from its threat model. Code/data are promised but not yet verified as released.
row.Evidence Locator: Sections 3.1-3.4, 4, 5.1-5.2, 6-10, and 12; Figure 1; full feature definitions in Appendix B; evasion methodology in Appendix D
row.Reproduction Status: Not attempted: public artifact not verified
row.Reproduction Evidence: arXiv HTML reproducibility paragraph states that code, trained models, processed datasets, feature extraction, and evaluation scripts will be made available upon publication
row.QA Flag: Do not generalize beyond API-driven browser automation; do not report simulated-bot aggregate metrics as real-bot evidence; artifact availability requires recheck
row.Authors: Vishisht Choudhary; Lukas Schmidt; Anne Zoë Kenntner; Feras Skhab; Michel Osswald; Jens Ernstberger
row.Related Seed: FP-Agent; Known By Their Actions; foundational mouse-dynamics literature
row.Research Role: Closest external behavioral agent-detection comparator and executor-confound warning
row.Observer Position: Website-side JavaScript/DOM event recorder plus offline session-level feature extractor
row.Observation Signal: mousemove, mousedown, mouseup, click, keydown, keyup, scroll, timestamps, isTrusted, missing raw-event sequences, and browser-environment indicators
row.Evaluation Setting: Controlled three-class benchmark, ten random seeds, three detector families, a five-level evasion ladder, task-domain ablation, and exhaustive feature-subset search
